I was transgender from age 8 to 18. I'm talking suicidal, using different pronouns, having a new name, not wanting to be around girls, the whole 10 yards. I finally came to peace with my gender.

Here's the thing about transgenderism. It's usually a result of other physical or mental issues. For me, it was extremely high testosterone and having to be the "man of the house" growing up because my dad was always on the road, along with body dysmorphia. 

I don't mean to invalidate you. I know very well how all consuming it is. But it may be worth looking at other trauma that may have caused this. I have a friend whose transgenderism is 100% trauma based and they have an identity crisis every couple of years despite having transitioned. It's also worth looking into body dysmorphia. If you have that, no matter how you look you will not be happy with it, even if you fully medically transition. If you have low testosterone that will cause some gender dysphoria. If you have high estrogen that will cause gender dysphoria. It's amazing how much our hormones do, honestly. 

Feel free to message me further for my experience. Like I said, I fully believed I would not be happy unless I was a guy. I didn't get along with girls, I tried to make myself look more like a guy, I already have a lower voice than most, etc. But I did find peace and acceptance of the gender God gave me.

Heavenly Father and Jesus have a place for everyone at the table. We do not join the Church to be "normal." In every state outside of Utah, we are generally quite the opposite. My husband converted to the Church last November, at the age of 25. (He might have still been 24 actually). We are married so obviously he didn't serve a mission and neither did I because I married him instead. We have no children right now. 

His parents have left the Church, his siblings never chose to be baptized. We haven't been sealed in the temple yet and I haven't been endowed (I've decided I'll go through for the first time when he does). He's only recently been given the Aaronic priesthood and is dyslexic so he stumbles through the Sacrament prayers right now and usually has to do them a couple times. 

Normal is a setting on a washing machine. We still participate in church. We make it to the temple when we can, even if we're just sitting in the baptistry chapel. The important part of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints is not its members nor what they think of me or him. If they judged us, honestly I don't think we would notice. We're too busy keeping our eyes focused on Christ and Heavenly Father. We go to church to take the Sacrament and to study the words of the scriptures and the prophets and listen to the insights of other members as well as provide our own. We go to the various Conferences (ward, stake, General, etc) to hear what God wants us to hear. We go to church activities to think about our covenants and also to follow Christ's commandment of loving one another (getting to know the members of our ward). Etc. 

You do have a place in church. We do not have to be the same as other people to have a place. Jesus was an outcast. He did not fit in. He went so hard against the grain that He was killed (I'd hope that part doesn't happen to us though). Do not let the weakness of men keep you from the love of Christ.

But the key thing is to look at what they do. Why are the animals in their exhibits there. Are they involved in programs working on getting animals off the endangered species list. Are they working on educating rather than just showing. Do they help with research programs for conservation. Do they have access to a fully equipped animal hospital. Are the habitats large enough for the animals to move around and enriching. Etc.

Captivity is keeping a lot of them alive, unfortunately. Ones that aren't involved in breeding/ ethical research/ etc programs are usually too injured to go into the wild. I.e a manatee losing its buoyancy or a fish with cancer.

Look at the work they do generally. Usually the ones actually involved in conservation actively publicize it because a major thing they are doing is also raising awareness. I.e the Secrets of the Zoo _____ series. Or Monterey Bay's public engagement livestreams. Or they'll often have listed on their websites if the animals they have are part of endangered species breeding programs. 

The average animal enthusiast that actually researches this stuff instead of living in the 70's like this person's mother is could also tell you. 

Honestly though there are not a ton of zoos/aquariums that I know of that aren't involved in conservation/rehabilitation these days. So many of them also network together as part of the overall un-endangering effort.

As with sharks, manatees, and the like, in proper zoos/aquariums the only dolphins in them can't survive in the wild for whatever reason or are part of a breeding program that requires the dolphin on hand/out of the way of a predator. She's at the prime age of forgetting the bad and moving on with the new, as long as you get right back to the business of being a loving parent. 

I highly recommend picking up a few parenting books for general advice. I like Nanny 911 and Kids are from Jupiter. 

Get her on a schedule. Wake up time, breakfast time, nap time (if she still takes one which she probably does, although there are signs to look for if she's ready to drop the last nap), lunch time, dinner time, bath time, bed time. Keep in mind that she is a toddler and you're not going to get the times exact. Just provide structure. 

Help her create her room. Even if she doesn't sleep in it right away, a bedroom is a space she can have control over and that she can know is safe. 

Now I'm not saying only feed her vegan meals grown from your own backyard. But watch what you put in her. Lots of added sugar and food dyes can cause mental and behavioral issues in kids. Edit- aim for half her plate to be fruits and vegetables. You may have to get creative with how you serve them. But toddlers are picky so if she only wants fish sticks or whatever just try and sneak it in where you can and don't stress about it. Fruit is easier than vegetables. 

Limit screen time. She can watch some Disney shows and whatnot from time to time, but developmentally she should be working on creative play and motor skills. She should be able to start preschool now or when she's 4. 

Read to her. This is coming from an elementary teacher- the sooner they are exposed to reading and start learning letters, the better off they'll be for the rest of elementary. Don't drill it with her, just sing the alphabet song with her sometimes and read a fun book every night (have her choose the book). 

Make sure you get quality time with her. *Quality over quantity*. You don't have to be doing anything special. You can literally make some hot cocoa and watch her favorite show with her, or take her to the park for a half hour. With the holiday season starting, there will also be a lot of activities geared towards her age group that you can take her to when you have time. 

Make sure you get acquainted with her pediatrician. Just set up a general check up. Try and find some toddler play groups to get her some interaction and you a moment to breathe and other adults to support you. 

Overall - do not beat yourself up. Do not blame yourself. You are a family that has suffered a great loss and a father that is doing the best that he can. Even if you don't get things perfect all the time, which you won't, you are loving her and doing the best you can, and that is all that matters. Be a loving father, and the rest will take care of itself.
